title: Diabetes pill that reduces blood sugar levels can also reduce heart risks in the elderly
text:
By Luke Chafer for Sunday mail
Published: 01:38 GMT, February 9, 2025 | Updated: 02:02 GMT, February 9, 2025
A diabetes pill that reduces blood sugar levels can also reduce the risk of heart attacks and stroke in older people, according to a study.
Experts are now asking for NHS guidance, which does not recommend managing diabetes with different medications depending on age, to update the light of the findings.
Tablets, collectively known as sodium-glucose-2 co-transporters, or SGLT2 inhibitors, are designed to reduce blood sugar levels.
More than four million people in the United Kingdom have been diagnosed with diabetes. Half of them are over 65 years old and a room exceed 75, while almost 15 percent of more than 85 have the condition.
Older people with diabetes have a higher risk of heart failure and stroke. SGLT2 inhibitors, which include the daily tablets Pagliflozina and Dapagliflozin already available in the NHS, help the kidneys eliminate excess sugar.
This helps fight the disease, but they also come with a variety of other health benefits, including the slowdown in kidney disease.

In June 2021, El Correo revealed on Sunday that an essay from the University of Leeds found that when patients with type 2 diabetes received opponent, seemed to strengthen the heart.
The last study, conducted by a group of researchers from the University of Glasgow, analyzed data from 300,000 patients. The meta -analysis evaluated 600 diabetes drug trials worldwide and discovered that SGLT2 was associated with a reduced risk of heart attacks and strokes in older people.
“Deciding the best treatments for the elderly always requires a careful balance of risks and benefits,” says Dr. Peter Hanlon, a member of Clinical Research at the University of Glasgow.
‘Our findings that the elderly experienced greater benefits of these drugs, in terms of heart attacks and reduced strokes, are very encouraging.
“Age alone should not be a barrier for treatments with proven benefits, provided they are well tolerated and aligned with patient priorities.”
